phy-m1s55.background: Forces add as arrows, not as numbers. If two forces pull in different directions you cannot simply total them, because part of each is spent pulling across the other. When the two happen to be at RIGHT ANGLES the arithmetic is at its kindest: neither has any component along the other, so the resultant is just the diagonal of the rectangle they make, which is Pythagoras.
given: F₁ = 320 N, directed upwards (from charge P)
F₂ = 120 N, directed to the left (from charge R)
The +8 µC on S is scene-setting and is NOT used
phy-m1s55.find: The resultant force on S: its size, and the angle it makes
phy-m1s55.formula: F = √(F₁² + F₂²),   tan θ = F₁ / F₂
phy-m1s55.why: Two perpendicular forces are being combined, and perpendicular means Pythagoras. The angle comes from the tangent, which is opposite over adjacent, so which force you put on top decides which angle you get. The question asks for the angle to the 120 N force, so the 320 N is the opposite side and goes on top.
symbols: F = the resultant, the single force that would do the same job as both
F₁ = 320 N, the upward force
F₂ = 120 N, the leftward force
θ = the angle measured from the 120 N force round to the resultant
steps: θ = tan⁻¹(2.667) = 69.44°, measured from the 120 N force
phy-m1s55.check: 116800 is sitting in the option list as an answer, which is what you get by stopping before the square root, so finish the job. And sanity-check the angle by eye: the 320 N force is much the bigger of the two, so the resultant must lean towards it, meaning an angle well over 45° from the 120 N. 69.44° leans the right way; the option offering 20.56° is the same angle measured from the wrong force.

phy-m1s57.background: Coulomb's law works in exactly the same shape as gravity, but with one extra freedom: charges can push as well as pull. Like signs repel, unlike signs attract, and the size of the force does not care which is which. So the routine is always two separate jobs: get the size from the formula, then get the direction from the signs.
phy-m1s57.find: The size of the force on the negative charge, and its direction
phy-m1s57.why: Two charges and a separation are named, which is the signature of Coulomb's law rather than F = qE. The signs are deliberately left out of the arithmetic: putting a minus into the formula gives a negative force, which is meaningless as a magnitude. Handle the sign in words instead.
symbols: F = the electrostatic force, in newtons
k = the Coulomb constant, 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
Q₁, Q₂ = the sizes of the two charges, in coulombs
r = their separation, in metres, and it is SQUARED
steps: r² = 1² = 1, so the bottom does nothing here
Direction: one charge is positive and the other negative, so they ATTRACT
The force on the negative charge points TOWARDS the 1 C charge
phy-m1s57.check: Four of the five options carry a plausible-looking number, so the direction is doing half the work of this question. Read the signs before you read the numbers: unlike signs means towards, like signs means away. Note also how large 1.26 × 10⁵ N is, about the weight of a lorry, which is why a whole coulomb of charge is never found sitting still in one place.

phy-m1s58.background: Newton's third law does not stop being true for electric forces. Whatever A does to B, B does back to A with equal size and opposite direction, no matter how unequal the two charges are. This surprises people, because a 4 nC charge feels like it ought to push harder than a 1 nC one. It does not, and the formula shows why: both charges appear in the SAME product, so there is only one force size to be had.
phy-m1s58.find: The size and direction of the force on A, and the force on B
phy-m1s58.why: Two charges and a separation again, so Coulomb's law. The important reading is that the formula produces ONE number, not one per charge. That single number is the force each feels, which is Newton's third law falling out of the algebra rather than being quoted separately.
symbols: F = the force each charge feels, in newtons
k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
Q₁, Q₂ = the two charges, here 1.0 nC and 4.0 nC, in coulombs
r = their separation, in metres, SQUARED
1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C, and 1 cm = 0.01 m
steps: Convert first:  1.0 nC = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ C,  4.0 nC = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C,  1.0 cm = 0.01 m
Direction: one negative, one positive, so ATTRACTIVE, each pulled towards the other
phy-m1s58.check: The wrong option that says B feels more because it has more charge is the exact misconception this question exists to catch. Squash it with the formula: Q_A and Q_B are multiplied together, so swapping which charge you call which changes nothing. Watch the centimetre too, since 1 cm squared is 10⁻⁴ and not 10⁻², and that slip moves the answer by two powers of ten straight into another option.

phy-c2-03.background: Potential difference is not really about volts as a substance; it is a statement about ENERGY PER COULOMB. Saying a battery is 12 V is saying that each coulomb passing through it gains 12 joules. So the work done on any amount of charge is just how many coulombs there are, times how many joules each one gets.
phy-c2-03.find: The work done W, in joules
phy-c2-03.why: This comes straight from the definition of the volt: one volt is one joule per coulomb. Multiply the volts by the coulombs and the coulombs cancel, leaving joules. Nothing else is needed, and in particular no distance or field, because a potential difference already has the distance built into it.
symbols: W = the work done, or the energy transferred, in joules
Q = the charge moved, in coulombs
V = the potential difference it moves through, in volts
phy-c2-03.check: Check by units, which is faster than re-doing the arithmetic. Coulombs × (joules per coulomb) = joules, so the units work out and the multiplication was the right operation. Had you divided you would have got 0.25, which is sitting in the option list waiting for exactly that mistake.

phy-s2-04.background: Between two parallel plates the field is UNIFORM, which means it has the same strength everywhere between them, unlike the field of a point charge which weakens with distance. That uniformity is what makes the plate formula so simple: the voltage is shared out evenly across the gap, so the field is just volts per metre. The unit V m⁻¹ is telling you the formula.
phy-s2-04.find: The field strength E between the plates, in V m⁻¹
phy-s2-04.why: Parallel plates with a stated voltage and separation is the signature of this formula. There is no inverse square here at all, because the field does not spread out: the plates are flat and the lines run straight across, so nothing gets diluted with distance.
symbols: E = the uniform field strength, in V m⁻¹, the same as N C⁻¹
V = the potential difference across the plates, in volts
d = the plate separation, in METRES, which is where the mark is lost
steps: Dividing by 10⁻³ is multiplying by 10³:  E = 30 × 10³
phy-s2-04.check: The option 30 V m⁻¹ is what you get by leaving the gap in millimetres, and it is the commonest answer given by people who did the physics correctly. Dividing by a SMALL number must give a BIG answer, so if your result looks similar in size to the 60 you started with, the conversion did not happen.

phy-c2-07.background: Gauss's law makes a claim that sounds too good to be true: the total flux out of a closed surface depends only on the charge INSIDE it, and not at all on charges outside, nor on where inside the charge sits, nor on the shape of the surface. The reason is that a field line from an outside charge that enters the surface must also leave it, so it contributes once as negative flux and once as positive and cancels itself out.
given: A separate 10 µC charge sits OUTSIDE the surface
phy-c2-07.find: The total electric flux Φ through the closed surface, in N m² C⁻¹
phy-c2-07.why: The surface is CLOSED, which is the word that summons Gauss's law rather than Φ = EA cos θ. The outside charge is a deliberate distractor: it certainly changes the field at every point on the surface, but it adds nothing to the TOTAL flux, because whatever enters also leaves.
symbols: Φ = the total flux through the closed surface, in N m² C⁻¹
Q = the ENCLOSED charge only, in coulombs
ε₀ = the permittivity of free space, 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹
steps: Enclosed charge only:  Q = 3 µC = 3 × 10⁻⁶ C
The 10 µC is outside, so it contributes zero net flux and is discarded
phy-c2-07.check: Two traps are in the options. Adding both charges gives 1.47 × 10⁶, and the zero option tempts anyone who thinks the outside charge cancels the inside one, which it does not: it cancels only itself. Ask one question of any Gauss problem before anything else, which is what is INSIDE, and the rest is one division.

phy-s3-01.background: Flux counts how much of a field actually passes through a surface. Hold a hoop square-on to the field and you catch everything; tilt it and you catch less; turn it edge-on and nothing goes through at all. The cosine does that job, but only if the angle is measured the way physics defines it, which is from the NORMAL, the line sticking straight out of the surface, not from the surface itself.
phy-s3-01.find: The electric flux Φ, in N m² C⁻¹
phy-s3-01.why: The surface is flat and open rather than closed, and the field is uniform, so this is the direct flux formula and not Gauss's law. Cosine rather than sine because at 0°, square-on, the flux must be at its maximum, and cos 0 = 1 while sin 0 = 0.
symbols: Φ = the electric flux, in N m² C⁻¹
E = the field strength, in N C⁻¹
A = the area, in m²
θ = the angle from the NORMAL to the surface
phy-s3-01.check: The option 400 is the flux you would get square-on, so it must be the maximum and cannot be right for a tilted surface: a tilt can only reduce the flux, never increase it. The option 346 is what sin 60° would have given, which is the standard punishment for using the wrong trigonometric function.

phy-m2s20.background: Capacitance is not only a property of two facing plates. Any isolated conductor has one, because putting charge on it raises its potential, and capacitance is simply the ratio of the two. For a sphere the answer depends on nothing but its radius: a bigger sphere spreads the same charge over more surface, so its potential rises less, so its capacitance is larger.
phy-m2s20.find: The capacitance C of the spherical shell, in farads
phy-m2s20.why: It follows from the two things already known about a sphere: its potential is V = kQ ÷ R, and capacitance is C = Q ÷ V. Divide one by the other and the Q cancels, leaving C = R ÷ k, which is the same as 4πε₀R because k = 1 ÷ (4πε₀). There is no second plate and no gap, so the parallel plate formula cannot apply.
symbols: C = the capacitance, in farads
ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹
R = the radius of the sphere, in METRES
4π = 12.566, a pure number
phy-m2s20.check: A one metre sphere, which is enormous, manages only about a hundred picofarads. That is worth remembering as a feel for the size of things: capacitance is hard to come by from geometry alone, which is exactly why real capacitors use large rolled-up areas and gaps measured in microns. The option 8.85 × 10⁻¹² is what you get by forgetting the 4π entirely.

phy-m2s23.background: A dielectric is an insulator slipped between the plates, and it improves a capacitor without any change of shape. Its molecules turn to face the field and set up a small field of their own pointing the other way, which partly cancels the original. Less net field means less voltage for the same charge, and less voltage for the same charge means more capacitance. The dielectric constant is simply the factor by which it helps.
given: C₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹¹ F, the capacitance with nothing between the plates
K = 3, the dielectric constant of the material inserted
phy-m2s23.find: The new capacitance C with the dielectric in place
phy-m2s23.why: The geometry is untouched, since neither the plate area nor the gap changes, so the only new ingredient is the material. Its whole effect is one multiplying factor. This is quicker and safer than rebuilding the capacitance from ε₀A ÷ d, and it works whatever the shape of the capacitor.
symbols: C = the capacitance with the dielectric, in farads
K = the dielectric constant, sometimes written εr, a pure number with no unit
C₀ = the original capacitance in vacuum or air, in farads
steps: Tidy into standard form:  C = 2.655 × 10⁻¹⁰ F
phy-m2s23.check: A dielectric can only INCREASE capacitance, because K is never less than 1 for any real material. So the answer must be bigger than 8.85 × 10⁻¹¹, which instantly kills the options offering 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ and 2.7 × 10⁻¹¹, both of which are smaller. The remaining care is tidying 26.55 × 10⁻¹¹ into 2.655 × 10⁻¹⁰, which is the same number.

phy-m3s06.background: Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point, which is charge divided by time. The word RATE is what matters: a large charge moving slowly can carry less current than a small charge moving quickly. And current is about CHARGE, so anything that is not charge, however fast it moves, carries no current at all.
given: Situation (c):  a person walking 8 m in 4 s
phy-m3s06.find: Which situation has the greatest electric current
phy-m3s06.why: Comparison questions are answered by computing each candidate on the same footing rather than by guessing from the raw numbers. Situation (a) has the larger charge, which invites the wrong answer, so the division must actually be done.
symbols: I = the current, in amperes, where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹
Q = the charge that flows, in coulombs
t = the time it takes, in seconds
steps: Situation (c):  a walking person moves mass, not charge, so I = 0
The answer is situation (b), at 3 A
phy-m3s06.check: Situation (a) has twice the charge of (b) and still loses, which is the whole point of the question: current is a rate, so the time matters as much as the charge. Situation (c) is there to test whether you noticed that metres per second is a speed and not a current. It would only carry current if the walker were charged.

phy-m3s08.background: Current is a flow of electrons, but it is measured in coulombs per second rather than electrons per second, because an electron carries an absurdly small charge. Converting between the two is always a two-step job: first find how many coulombs flowed, then ask how many electrons that many coulombs is. Trying to do it in one step is where the error creeps in.
given: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the charge on one electron
phy-m3s08.find: The number of electrons n that pass through the drive
phy-m3s08.formula: Q = It,   then   n = Q / e
phy-m3s08.why: Two formulas because there are two conversions. The first turns a current and a time into a charge, which is just the definition of current rearranged. The second turns that charge into a count, using the fact that charge comes in fixed lumps of size e. Neither can be skipped.
symbols: Q = the total charge that flowed, in coulombs
I = the current, in amperes
t = the time, in seconds
n = the number of electrons, a pure count
e = the elementary charge, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
steps: Step one, the charge:  Q = I × t
Step two, the count:  n = Q ÷ e
phy-m3s08.check: The option 0.99 × 10¹⁸ is a trap for stopping after step one and then decorating the charge with a power of ten. Notice the number 6.2 × 10¹⁸: it is the same figure that appears in the charge-quantisation question, because 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons is what makes one coulomb. Since 0.99 C is very nearly one coulomb, the count had to come out near that value.

phy-m3s18.background: A battery does work on every coulomb it pushes round the circuit, and the emf says how much: 1.5 V means 1.5 joules given to each coulomb. So finding the total work is again a two-step job. First find how many coulombs went round, then multiply by the joules each one received. The energy did not come from nowhere; it came out of the chemicals inside the cell.
phy-m3s18.find: The charge that passes, in coulombs, and the work done, in joules
phy-m3s18.why: The current and the time give the charge, because current is charge per second. The charge and the voltage then give the energy, because voltage is energy per coulomb. Each formula is a definition read the other way round, which is why they chain together so neatly.
symbols: Q = the charge that circulates, in coulombs
I = the current, in amperes
t = the time, in seconds
W = the work done by the battery, in joules
V = the emf, the energy given per coulomb, in volts
phy-m3s18.check: One option offers the same two numbers the other way round, 42 C and 28 J, so read your own labels before choosing. A quick guard: the emf is 1.5, which is more than 1, so the work in joules must be LARGER than the charge in coulombs. 42 is larger than 28, so the pairing is the right way round.

phy-m3s23.background: Ohm's law is the most-used relation in the whole of electricity, and it is worth seeing it as a statement about push and opposition. The voltage is the push, the resistance is the opposition, and the current is what results. Push harder and more flows; oppose more and less flows.
phy-m3s23.find: The current I through the resistor, in amperes
phy-m3s23.why: A voltage and a resistance are given and a current is wanted, which is Ohm's law arranged with I on the left. There is only one component, so no combining of resistances is needed first.
symbols: I = the current, in amperes
V = the potential difference across the resistor, in volts
R = the resistance, in ohms
phy-m3s23.check: The resistance in ohms is much bigger than the voltage in volts, so the current must come out well BELOW one amp. That single glance rules out 6.25 A and 3600 A before any arithmetic. Among the survivors, 0.016 differs from 0.16 by a factor of ten, so count the decimal places carefully: 24 ÷ 150 is a bit more than 24 ÷ 240, which is 0.1.

phy-m3s37.background: In a series circuit the same current passes through every component, because there is only one path for it to take. That makes the whole string behave like one big resistor whose value is the simple total. So if you know the supply voltage and the current, Ohm's law hands you that total, and anything missing from the string can then be found by subtraction.
given: All three resistors are in SERIES
phy-m3s37.find: The resistance of R₃, in ohms
phy-m3s37.formula: R = V over I,   then   R₃ = R − R₁ − R₂
phy-m3s37.why: Working backwards is the trick here. Ohm's law applied to the whole circuit gives the total resistance, because in series the current through the whole loop is the current the battery supplies. Once the total is known, the unknown resistor is whatever is left after removing the two you were told.
symbols: R = the total resistance of the series string, in ohms
V = the battery voltage, in volts
I = the current, the SAME everywhere in a series loop
R₁, R₂, R₃ = the three individual resistances
steps: Total resistance from Ohm's law:  R = V ÷ I
phy-m3s37.check: The 750 is deliberately offered as an option, so do not stop at the total. Verify forwards in one line: 250 + 150 + 350 = 750, and 24 ÷ 750 = 0.032 A, which is the current given. That closes the loop and proves the answer.

phy-m3s46.background: In parallel, every resistor is connected straight across the battery, so every one of them gets the FULL supply voltage. They do not share it. What they share is the current, each taking as much as its own resistance allows, and the battery has to supply the total. That is why adding more parallel branches makes the circuit draw more current, not less.
given: R₁ = 250.0 Ω, R₂ = 150.0 Ω, R₃ = 350.0 Ω, all in PARALLEL
V = 24.0 V across all of them
phy-m3s46.find: The total current supplied by the battery, in amperes
phy-m3s46.formula: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃,  where each  I = V / R
phy-m3s46.why: There are two valid routes and this is the safer one. You could combine the resistances with reciprocals first and then divide once, but that means three reciprocals and a final flip, which is four chances to slip. Finding each branch current separately and adding uses only division and addition, and it also shows which branch carries most, which is often the next part of the question.
symbols: I = the total current drawn from the battery, in amperes
I₁, I₂, I₃ = the currents in the three branches
V = 24.0 V, the same across EVERY branch in parallel
R₁, R₂, R₃ = the branch resistances, in ohms
phy-m3s46.check: Every individual branch current is offered as a wrong option, so make sure you added rather than stopping at one of them. Two guards on the result: the total must be LARGER than the biggest single branch current, and here 0.325 comfortably exceeds 0.160. And compare with the series version of the same three resistors, which drew only 0.032 A, ten times less. Parallel always draws more.

phy-m3s51.background: Most real circuits are neither purely series nor purely parallel, but a mixture, and the way through is always the same: find a group that is clearly one or the other, replace it with a single equivalent resistor, and repeat until only one resistor is left. Work from the inside out, and never try to see the whole circuit in one go.
given: Two of them are in series with each other
That pair is in parallel with the third
phy-m3s51.find: The current supplied by the battery, in amperes
phy-m3s51.why: The series pair goes first, because it is the innermost group: two resistors one after the other simply add, giving 900 Ω. That 900 Ω branch and the remaining 450 Ω branch span the same two points, so they are in parallel, and the product-over-sum form is the quickest way to combine exactly two resistors. Ohm's law then finishes it.
symbols: R₁, R₂ = the two BRANCHES being combined in parallel, here 900 Ω and 450 Ω
R = their combined resistance, always SMALLER than either branch
I = the current from the battery, in amperes
steps: Now parallel with the third:  R = (900 × 450) ÷ (900 + 450)
phy-m3s51.check: The parallel result must be smaller than both branches, and 300 is duly under 450 and under 900. Two wrong routes appear in the options: treating all three as one series string gives 1350 Ω and a current of 0.0089 A, while treating all three as parallel gives 150 Ω and 0.080 A. The correct answer sits between them, which is exactly where a mixed circuit should land.

phy-m3s55.background: When resistors sit in series they share the supply voltage between them, and they share it in proportion to their resistance. The bigger resistor takes the bigger share, because the same current passes through both and V = IR. This is called a voltage divider, and it is how a circuit produces a smaller voltage from a larger one without a transformer.
given: R₂ = 10 kΩ, in series with R₁
phy-m3s55.find: The voltage across R₂, in volts
phy-m3s55.why: The divider rule is the same physics as finding the current and multiplying by R₂, but written as one line so there is only one chance to slip. Read it as a fraction: R₂ over the total is the SHARE that R₂ takes, and that share of the supply voltage is what appears across it.
symbols: V₂ = the voltage across R₂, in volts
V = the total supply voltage, in volts
R₂ = the resistance you want the voltage across
R₁ + R₂ = the total series resistance
1 kΩ = 1000 Ω, but the k cancels here so it can stay
phy-m3s55.check: R₂ is the smaller resistor, so it must take the SMALLER share, meaning under half of 20 V. 8.0 V is under 10, so it leans the right way; the option 12.0 V is the share belonging to R₁, offered for anyone who put the wrong resistance on top. Check the pair adds up: 8 + 12 = 20 V, the full supply, with nothing unaccounted for. Note the kilohms never had to be converted, because the same unit appears on top and bottom and cancels.

phy-m3s57.background: Power is the rate at which a resistor turns electrical energy into heat, and it has three forms, P = VI, P = I²R and P = V² ÷ R. They are the same equation with Ohm's law substituted in, so all three always agree. Choose whichever one matches what you have been given, since that avoids an intermediate step and an intermediate chance to slip.
phy-m3s57.find: The total power dissipated, in watts
phy-m3s57.why: The supply voltage and the total resistance are both known, so this form gets there in one step. There is a shortcut worth seeing: the TOTAL power can be found from the total resistance directly, without ever computing V₁ and V₂ separately, because the two resistors share the same current and the powers simply add.
symbols: P = the total power dissipated as heat, in watts
V = the supply voltage, in volts, and it is SQUARED
R = the total series resistance, in ohms
phy-m3s57.check: Verify the long way in two lines to prove the shortcut. The current is I = 20 ÷ 800 = 0.025 A, so V₁ = 0.025 × 470 = 11.75 V and V₂ = 0.025 × 330 = 8.25 V, which correctly add to 20 V. Then P₁ = 11.75 × 0.025 = 0.294 W and P₂ = 8.25 × 0.025 = 0.206 W, and those add to 0.5 W. Both of those partial powers are sitting in the option list, so make sure you gave the TOTAL.

phy-m3s67.background: A current source is the mirror image of a voltage source: it insists on pushing a fixed current out, and lets the voltage settle wherever the circuit requires. So the reasoning runs the other way round from usual. Instead of starting with a voltage and finding the current, you start with the current, find the resistance it faces, and multiply.
given: I = 20 mA = 0.020 A, from a current source
R₁ = 100 Ω and R₂ = 200 Ω, in PARALLEL
phy-m3s67.find: The voltage across R₂, in volts
phy-m3s67.why: The whole 20 mA has to pass through the parallel combination, so the voltage that appears across it is the source current times the combined resistance. And because the two resistors are in parallel, that same voltage sits across BOTH of them, so once you have it for the pair you have it for R₂ without any further work.
symbols: R = the combined parallel resistance, in ohms
R₁, R₂ = the two resistors, in ohms
I = the source current, in amperes
V = the voltage across the pair, which is the voltage across each
phy-m3s67.check: In parallel the voltage is common, so the answer for R₂ is identical to the answer for R₁; if you found yourself splitting the current first, you took a longer road to the same place. Guard the parallel step: 66.67 Ω is smaller than both 100 and 200, as any parallel combination must be. Using 300 Ω instead, by adding as if in series, would give 6 V, and using only R₂ would give 4 V, which is duly offered as a trap.

phy-m3s92.background: Kirchhoff's two laws are just conservation restated for circuits. The junction law says charge cannot pile up at a junction, so whatever flows in must flow out. The loop law says energy cannot be created going round a loop, so the voltage rises and drops must cancel. For two resistors fed by a current source, both laws are visible at once: the currents split at the junction, and both resistors share one voltage.
given: The two resistors are in parallel
phy-m3s92.find: The current I₁ in the 8 Ω resistor, and the voltage V across the pair
phy-m3s92.why: Find the voltage first and the currents come free. The 10 A must cross the parallel combination, so V = IR gives the shared voltage in one step, and then each branch current is that voltage divided by its own resistance. Trying to split the current first means using the current divider rule, which is easy to get upside down.
symbols: R = the combined parallel resistance, in ohms
V = the voltage across the pair, common to both branches
I₁ = the current in the 8 Ω branch, in amperes
I₂ = the current in the 4 Ω branch, in amperes
steps: Branch two, for the check:  I₂ = 26.67 ÷ 4 = 6.67 A
phy-m3s92.check: Kirchhoff's junction law is the check, and it costs one line: I₁ + I₂ = 3.33 + 6.67 = 10 A, which is exactly what the source supplies, so nothing has been lost or invented. A second guard by eye: the SMALLER resistor must take the BIGGER current, so the 4 Ω branch should carry more than the 8 Ω branch, and 6.67 duly exceeds 3.33. The option offering 6.67 A for I₁ has the two branches swapped.

phy-m3s93.background: When a circuit has more than one loop, Kirchhoff's laws are the general tool, but a circuit that is only series and parallel underneath can be unpicked more quickly by reduction. Collapse the parallel part into one resistor, find the total current, then expand back out to recover the individual branch currents. Reduce, solve, expand.
given: R₁ = 10 Ω, carrying I₁, in series with the rest
6 Ω and 4 Ω in series carrying I₃, forming a branch parallel to R₂
phy-m3s93.why: The 6 Ω and 4 Ω sit one after the other in the same branch, so they add to a single 10 Ω before anything else happens. That branch and the 8 Ω branch span the same two nodes, so they combine in parallel. What is left is the 10 Ω of R₁ in series with that combination, which is a single loop Ohm's law can finish.
symbols: R₃ = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω, the series branch treated as one resistor
Rp = the parallel combination of R₂ and R₃, in ohms
I₁ = the total current from the source, in amperes
I₃ = the current in the 6 Ω and 4 Ω branch, which is what we want
steps: Collapse the series branch:  R₃ = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω
Parallel it with R₂:  Rp = (8 × 10) ÷ (8 + 10) = 80 ÷ 18 = 4.444 Ω
Total round the loop:  R = R₁ + Rp = 10 + 4.444 = 14.444 Ω
Voltage across the parallel part:  Vp = I₁ × Rp = 3.462 × 4.444
Expand back out:  I₃ = Vp ÷ R₃ = 15.385 ÷ 10
phy-m3s93.check: Recover the other branch and test the junction: I₂ = 15.385 ÷ 8 = 1.923 A, and I₂ + I₃ = 1.923 + 1.538 = 3.461 A, which matches the total current I₁ to three decimals. Sense check as well: the 10 Ω branch has more resistance than the 8 Ω branch, so it must carry LESS current, and 1.538 is duly below 1.923.

phy-m4s84.background: A real cell is a perfect source of emf with a small resistance built in, and that internal resistance is not a defect to be ignored but the reason a battery's voltage sags under load. The emf must drive the current through the outside circuit AND through the cell itself, so the two resistances are met one after the other and simply add.
phy-m4s84.find: The emf E of the cell, in volts
phy-m4s84.why: This is Ohm's law applied to the complete loop rather than to one component. The current is the same everywhere in a single loop, so the total opposition it meets is R + r, and the emf is what pushes it through both.
symbols: E = the emf, the full push generated by the cell, in volts
I = the current in the loop, in amperes
R = the external or load resistance, in ohms
r = the internal resistance of the cell, in ohms
steps: Add the resistances:  R + r = 5 + 0.5 = 5.5 Ω
phy-m4s84.check: The emf must exceed the terminal p.d., which here is IR = 1 × 5 = 5 V. It does, by exactly the 0.5 V lost inside. The option 5.0 V is that terminal p.d. offered as a trap for anyone who forgot the cell's own resistance. This same question was set again in test 2, which tells you the examiner likes it.

phy-m4s86.background: Read from the other end, the same cell idea asks you to rebuild the emf from what actually reached the outside world. The terminal p.d. is what got out; the volts lost inside are Ir; add them and you have the full push. What makes it a step harder is that the current is not given, so it has to be found first.
phy-m4s86.find: The emf E of the cell, in volts
phy-m4s86.why: The terminal p.d. is the voltage across the external resistor, so Ohm's law on R alone gives the current. Only then can the lost volts be worked out. Jumping straight to E = I(R + r) is not wrong, but it needs the same current first, so nothing is saved.
symbols: E = the emf, in volts
V = the terminal p.d., what the outside circuit receives, in volts
I = the current, found from V and R
r = the internal resistance, in ohms
Ir = the volts lost inside the cell
steps: The terminal p.d. sits across R, so:  I = V ÷ R
phy-m4s86.check: Cross-check by the other route:  E = I(R + r) = 0.2 × 7 = 1.4 V. Agreement from two independent formulas is worth the one line it costs. Sanity: the emf must be bigger than the 1 V that got out, and 1.4 is. This question was also set in test 2, word for word.

phy-m4s89.background: Every question in this family is the same equation, E = I(R + r), read with a different unknown. Here the emf and the current are known and the internal resistance is the mystery, so the algebra runs backwards, but the physics has not changed at all. Recognising the family saves you from learning four separate formulas.
phy-m4s89.find: The internal resistance r of the battery, in ohms
phy-m4s89.why: One equation with one unknown, so it can simply be rearranged. Divide by the current to get the total resistance, then subtract the part you already know. That two-move pattern, total then subtract, is the same one used to find a missing resistor in a series string.
symbols: E = the emf, in volts
I = the current, in amperes
R = the external resistance, in ohms
r = the internal resistance, the unknown
steps: Divide both sides by I:  R + r = E ÷ I
phy-m4s89.check: Substitute back:  E = 1 × (4 + 2) = 6 V, which is the emf given, so the answer stands. The option 6 Ω is the TOTAL resistance offered as a trap for stopping one line early, and 10 Ω is what adding gives instead of subtracting.

phy-m4s90.background: This is the standard experiment for measuring what is inside a cell without opening it. Take two readings with different loads and you get two equations; the two unknowns, the emf and the internal resistance, then fall out together. It works because the emf is a fixed property of the cell while the terminal p.d. changes with the load, and the difference between them is always Ir.
given: First reading:  V = 12 V with R = 20 Ω
Second reading:  V = 13.5 V with R = 45 Ω
phy-m4s90.find: The emf E of the battery, in volts
phy-m4s90.formula: E = V + Ir,  where  I = V / R
phy-m4s90.why: One reading is not enough, because it gives one equation with two unknowns. A second reading gives a second equation, and since E and r are the same cell in both, setting the two expressions for E equal eliminates E and leaves r alone. This is simultaneous equations doing exactly what they are for.
symbols: E = the emf, the same in both readings
r = the internal resistance, also the same in both
V = the terminal p.d. for that reading, in volts
R = the external resistance for that reading, in ohms
I = the current for that reading, found as V ÷ R
steps: The cell is the same, so set them equal:  12 + 0.6r = 13.5 + 0.3r
Put r back into either equation:  E = 12 + 0.6 × 5
phy-m4s90.check: Test r = 5 in the OTHER equation, the one you did not use to finish:  E = 13.5 + 0.3 × 5 = 13.5 + 1.5 = 15 V. Both agree, so the pair is consistent. Sense check: the emf must exceed both terminal readings, and 15 is above 13.5 and above 12. Notice also the physical story, that the larger load resistance drew less current, so less was lost inside and the terminal reading climbed closer to the true emf.

phy-m4s35.background: A charged particle fired across a magnetic field is pushed sideways, and because the push stays sideways as the particle turns, it never speeds up or slows down. It just curls into a circle. Two questions follow naturally: how hard is the push, and how tight is the circle. The first is the force formula, the second comes from setting that force equal to what a circle requires.
given: v = 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, entering PERPENDICULAR to the field
phy-m4s35.find: The magnetic force F, in newtons, and the radius r of the path, in metres
phy-m4s35.why: Perpendicular entry means θ = 90° and sin 90° = 1, so the angle drops out of the force formula entirely. The radius formula comes from qvB = mv² ÷ r: the magnetic force IS the centripetal force, since it is the only force acting. Cancel one v and rearrange.
symbols: F = the magnetic force, in newtons
q = the charge on the proton, in coulombs
v = its speed, in m s⁻¹
B = the flux density, in teslas
m = the proton mass, in kilograms
r = the radius of the circular path, in metres
steps: Force first:  F = q × v × B
phy-m4s35.check: Cross-check the two answers against each other using the third relation, F = mv² ÷ r:  (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × (2 × 10⁶)²) ÷ 0.0418 = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 4 × 10¹²) ÷ 0.0418 = 6.68 × 10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 0.0418 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N, matching the force found first. A 4 cm circle is also a believable laboratory size, whereas the option offering 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ m would be a quarter of a millimetre.

phy-m4s36.background: When a particle enters a field at an angle rather than square on, split its velocity into two parts and treat them separately. The part ACROSS the field feels the magnetic force and curls into a circle. The part ALONG the field feels no force at all, since a charge moving parallel to the field is not cut by it, so it just carries on at constant speed. A circle plus a steady drift along the axis is a helix, like a stretched spring.
given: θ = 60° between the velocity and the field
phy-m4s36.find: Which velocity component sets the RADIUS, and which sets the PITCH
phy-m4s36.formula: r = m v sin θ over (qB)
phy-m4s36.why: The formula itself answers the question. Only the perpendicular component appears in it, so only v sin θ can affect the radius. The pitch, which is how far the helix advances along the field in one full turn, is set by the parallel component v cos θ multiplied by the time for one revolution, because that is the part doing the advancing.
symbols: v sin θ = the component ACROSS the field, which is bent into the circle
v cos θ = the component ALONG the field, which is never bent
r = the radius of the helix, in metres
the pitch = the advance along the field per complete turn, in metres
steps: Split the velocity at the angle to the FIELD:
Across the field:  v sin 60° = 3.5 × 10⁶ × 0.866 = 3.03 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
Along the field:  v cos 60° = 3.5 × 10⁶ × 0.5 = 1.75 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
The across part feels the force qvB and curls, so it sets the RADIUS
The along part feels no force and drifts, so it sets the PITCH
Answer: v sin 60 sets the radius, v cos 60 sets the pitch
phy-m4s36.check: Test the two extremes, which settles it without memorising. At θ = 90°, straight across the field, sin 90 = 1 and cos 90 = 0, so the radius is at its largest and the pitch is zero: a flat circle, which is right. At θ = 0°, straight along the field, sin 0 = 0 so there is no circle at all and the particle flies straight: infinite pitch, zero radius, also right. Only the sine-for-radius pairing survives both tests.

phy-m4s50.background: Current in a straight wire wraps a magnetic field around itself in circles. Grip the wire with your right hand, thumb pointing along the current, and your fingers curl the way the field points. The strength falls off as 1 over r, not as the inverse square, because a wire is a line rather than a point: move away and there is always more wire stretching off in both directions to make up for the distance.
phy-m4s50.find: The magnetic field B at that point, in teslas
phy-m4s50.why: Long straight conductor is the phrase that selects this formula. The 2πr underneath is the circumference of the field circle you are standing on: the field spreads itself around that circle, so a bigger circle means a weaker field. The solenoid formula has no π underneath at all, which is the quickest way to tell the two apart.
symbols: B = the field at that distance, in teslas
μ₀ = the permeability of free space, 4π × 10⁻⁷
I = the current, in amperes
r = the perpendicular distance from the wire, in metres, NOT squared
2πr = the circumference of the circular field line
steps: Cancel π top and bottom before anything else:
phy-m4s50.check: Learn the shortcut this cancelling reveals: μ₀ ÷ 2π is exactly 2 × 10⁻⁷, so B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × I ÷ r every time for a straight wire. That one substitution removes the commonest slip, which is keying 4π as 4 and then multiplying by π again. Sanity: 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ T is roughly the Earth's own field, which is the right order for a domestic current a few centimetres away.

phy-m4s63.background: The same straight wire law, with different numbers, which is the point of setting it twice: the routine should become automatic. Convert the centimetres, use μ₀ ÷ 2π = 2 × 10⁻⁷ so no π ever reaches the calculator, then divide by the distance to the first power.
phy-m4s63.find: The magnetic field B at 4 cm from the wire, in teslas
phy-m4s63.why: A straight conductor and a perpendicular distance, so the same formula as before. Nothing about a bigger current or a shorter distance changes which law applies; they only change the numbers that go into it.
symbols: B = the field, in teslas
I = the current, in amperes
r = the distance from the wire, in metres
μ₀ ÷ 2π = 2 × 10⁻⁷ exactly, worth using as a single constant
steps: Use the shortcut form:  B = (2 × 10⁻⁷ × I) ÷ r
phy-m4s63.check: Compare with the previous question as a cross-check on the physics. There, 12 A at 5 cm gave 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ T. Here the current is 1.25 times larger and the distance 0.8 times as far, so the field should be 1.25 ÷ 0.8 = 1.5625 times stronger. And 4.8 × 1.5625 = 7.5, which is exactly what came out. Proportional reasoning like that catches an arithmetic slip in seconds.

phy-s7-04.background: A current loop behaves like a tiny bar magnet, and its magnetic moment measures how strongly. Three things make it stronger: more current, more area enclosed, and more turns, because each turn adds its own contribution on top of the others. That is why a compass needle can be replaced by a coil, and why motors use many turns rather than one.
phy-s7-04.find: The magnetic dipole moment m, in A m²
phy-s7-04.why: The unit gives the formula away: A m² is amperes times metres squared, so it must be current times area, and the turns multiply because each one contributes equally. No field appears in the question, and none is needed, because the moment is a property of the loop itself and exists before any field is applied.
symbols: m = the magnetic dipole moment, in A m²
N = the number of turns
I = the current, in amperes
A = the area enclosed by ONE turn, in m²
phy-s7-04.check: Reconstruct the unit as the check: amperes × metres squared = A m², which matches what was asked for, so the multiplication was the right operation. The option 0.0008 is what you get by forgetting the 50 turns, and the turns are exactly why a coil is used instead of a single loop.

phy-s8-02.background: In B = μ₀nI the letter n does not mean the number of turns. It means turns PER METRE, the packing density. This matters because the field inside a solenoid depends on how tightly the wire is wound, not on how much wire there is: stretch the same 1500 turns over twice the length and the field halves.
phy-s8-02.find: The value of n to put into B = μ₀nI, with its unit
phy-s8-02.why: Whenever a solenoid question gives you a LENGTH, that length is there to convert the total turns into turns per metre. If you finish a solenoid problem without having used the length, you have almost certainly fed in N by mistake.
symbols: n = turns per metre, with the unit m⁻¹
N = the total number of turns, a pure count with no unit
L = the length of the solenoid, in metres
steps: Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2
phy-s8-02.check: The unit is the mark here. Two of the options give the number 3000, but one of them calls it 3000 turns in total, which is wrong: there are only 1500 turns, packed at 3000 per metre because the solenoid is half a metre long. Read the unit on the option, not just the digits. Note too that n came out larger than N, which always happens when the solenoid is shorter than a metre.

phy-s9-02.background: Push a rod across a magnetic field and the free electrons inside it are dragged sideways by the magnetic force, piling up at one end. That separation of charge is a voltage, and it lasts as long as the motion does. This is motional emf, and it is Faraday's law in disguise: as the rod moves, the area of the circuit it sweeps out grows, so the flux through that circuit changes.
given: L = 0.25 m, the length of the rod
B = 0.2 T, and the rod cuts the lines SQUARELY
phy-s9-02.why: Cutting the lines squarely means all three are mutually perpendicular, so there is no sine or cosine to apply and the three simply multiply. This is the shortcut form of Faraday's law for a straight conductor; the general ΔΦ ÷ Δt version would need the swept area and the time, which the question does not give directly.
symbols: emf = the induced voltage, in volts
B = the flux density, in teslas
L = the length of rod inside the field, in metres
v = the speed at which it moves, in m s⁻¹
phy-s9-02.check: Check by units, which is the reliable guard here: tesla × metre × (metre per second) works out to volts, so the three quantities were meant to be multiplied. Sense check the size too: a fifth of a volt from a quarter-metre rod at walking pace is a reminder of why real generators use many turns and spin fast, since one rod moving slowly produces very little.

phy-s9-04.background: An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field it creates, and the field cannot appear instantly: while the current is climbing, the coil induces a back-emf opposing the climb, and the work done against that back-emf is what ends up stored. Open the switch and the field collapses, returning the energy, which is why switching off an inductive load makes a spark.
phy-s9-04.find: The energy U stored in the inductor, in joules
phy-s9-04.why: An inductance and a current given, an energy wanted, and this is the only relation between the three. Notice the family resemblance to the capacitor's U = ½CV²: a half, the device property, and the square of what flows through or sits across it. Remembering one pattern gives you both.
symbols: U = the stored energy, in joules
L = the inductance, in henries
I = the current, in amperes, and it is SQUARED
phy-s9-04.check: The option 12 J is what you get by forgetting the square and computing ½ × 4 × 3 × 2, and 36 J is what you get by forgetting the half. Both wrong routes are in the list, so make sure both the half and the square survived. Guard by proportion: triple the current and the energy would rise ninefold, not threefold.

phy-m4s104.background: Faraday's law is about the RATE at which flux changes, not about how much flux there is. A coil sitting in the strongest field in the world produces nothing if nothing is changing. What is more, every turn of the coil experiences the same change, and their emfs add in series, so a coil of 200 turns produces 200 times the emf of a single loop. That is the whole reason coils are wound rather than left as single rings.
given: Flux falls from Φ₁ = 0.08 Wb to Φ₂ = 0.02 Wb
phy-m4s104.find: The magnitude of the induced emf, in volts
phy-m4s104.why: A flux change, a time and a number of turns are exactly the three quantities Faraday's law needs. The minus sign belongs to Lenz's law and states the direction, meaning the induced effect opposes the change that caused it; since the question asks only for the size, work with the magnitude of the change.
symbols: emf = the induced voltage, in volts
N = the number of turns, which MULTIPLIES the result
ΔΦ = the change in flux, in webers, taken as final minus initial
Δt = the time over which the change happens, in seconds
steps: Rate of change:  ΔΦ ÷ Δt = 0.06 ÷ 0.10 = 0.6 Wb s⁻¹
phy-m4s104.check: The option 0.6 V is the rate of change before multiplying by the turns, which is the commonest omission, and it is sitting there waiting. Ask two questions of every Faraday problem: did I divide by the TIME, and did I multiply by the TURNS. Note also that a modest flux change of 0.06 Wb yields 120 V purely because of the 200 turns, which is exactly how a real generator reaches useful voltages.

phy-m5s29.background: Maxwell's greatest result was not a new experiment but a piece of arithmetic. He combined his four equations, found they predicted a wave, and computed its speed from two constants measured in entirely electrical and magnetic experiments, with no light involved. The number that came out was the measured speed of light, which is how light was discovered to be an electromagnetic wave.
phy-m5s29.find: The wave speed v, in m s⁻¹
phy-m5s29.why: The two constants come from measurements with magnets and with capacitors, and neither has anything to do with light, which is what makes the result so striking. Do the product first, then the square root, then the reciprocal; changing that order is the usual source of error.
symbols: v = the speed of the electromagnetic wave in free space, in m s⁻¹
μ₀ = the permeability of free space, from magnetic measurements
ε₀ = the permittivity of free space, from electric measurements
c = the accepted symbol once you recognise the answer as the speed of light
steps: v = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, which is the speed of light c
phy-m5s29.check: Taking a square root of a power of ten needs the exponent to be EVEN, so rewrite 1.112 × 10⁻¹⁷ as 11.12 × 10⁻¹⁸ before rooting, and the root is √11.12 × 10⁻⁹ = 3.336 × 10⁻⁹. The option 3.34 × 10⁻⁹ is what you get by stopping before the reciprocal, and 8.99 × 10⁹ is the Coulomb constant wandering in from another topic. You should recognise 3 × 10⁸ on sight, which makes this question answerable in five seconds.

phy-m5s36.background: An electromagnetic wave carries an electric field and a magnetic field locked together, at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. They rise and fall in step, and their sizes are not independent: the ratio of the two is always the speed of light. That is why the magnetic part of light is so small a number, and why light is usually described by its electric field alone.
given: E₀ = 0.080 V m⁻¹, the electric field amplitude
phy-m5s36.find: The magnetic field amplitude B₀, in teslas
phy-m5s36.formula: E₀ / B₀ = c,   so   B₀ = E₀ / c
phy-m5s36.why: For any plane wave in free space the two amplitudes are tied by the speed of light, so one gives the other immediately with no wavelength, frequency or power needed. Dividing by such a large number is what makes B₀ tiny, which is the physical point rather than an arithmetic accident.
symbols: E₀ = the electric field amplitude, in V m⁻¹
B₀ = the magnetic field amplitude, in teslas
c = the speed of light in vacuum, 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
steps: Write the top in standard form:  0.080 = 8.0 × 10⁻²
phy-m5s36.check: Multiplying instead of dividing gives 2.4 × 10⁷ T, which is offered as an option and is physically absurd: the strongest laboratory magnets manage a few tens of teslas. Whenever you divide by c the answer must come out very SMALL, and whenever you multiply by c it must come out very large. That single habit sorts this whole family of questions.

phy-m5s43.background: Intensity is power spread over area, which is why a laser feels dangerous and a light bulb of the same wattage does not. The bulb throws its power over a whole room; the laser concentrates it into a spot a few millimetres across. Same watts, wildly different intensity, and it is the intensity that does the damage.
phy-m5s43.find: The intensity I, in W m⁻²
phy-m5s43.why: Intensity is defined as power per unit area, so this is the definition rather than a derived result. The only real work is the conversion of milliwatts to watts, which must happen before the division.
symbols: I = the intensity, in watts per square metre
P = the power, in watts
A = the cross-sectional area of the beam, in m²
phy-m5s43.check: The option 1.667 is what you get by leaving the power in milliwatts, and it is the one most people pick. Feel the size of the answer: 1667 W m⁻² is above the roughly 1000 W m⁻² of full sunlight, from a 5 mW pointer, which is precisely why you must never aim one at an eye. If your answer had come out around 1 W m⁻², the conversion did not happen.

phy-m5s45.background: The energy in an electromagnetic wave is carried by its fields, and the intensity is what the fields deliver per second per square metre. The relation involves E₀ SQUARED, so doubling the field quadruples the intensity, which is the same square law that appears in every wave in physics. Going backwards from intensity to field therefore needs a square root.
given: I = 1667 W m⁻², carried over from the previous part
phy-m5s45.find: The electric field amplitude E₀, in V m⁻¹
phy-m5s45.why: It is I = ½ε₀cE₀² rearranged for E₀. The half moves across as a doubling on top, ε₀c moves to the bottom, and the square comes off as a square root. Do it as one rearranged formula rather than in pieces, because each move is a chance to lose the factor of two.
symbols: E₀ = the electric field amplitude, in V m⁻¹
I = the intensity, in W m⁻²
ε₀ = the permittivity of free space
c = the speed of light, in m s⁻¹
the 2 = what is left of the half after rearranging
phy-m5s45.check: The option 2.655 × 10⁻³ is the value of ε₀c, offered to catch anyone who stopped mid-calculation, and 628 V m⁻¹ is roughly what dropping the factor of 2 would give. Cross-check forwards in one line: ½ × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 3 × 10⁸ × 1120² = ½ × 2.655 × 10⁻³ × 1.2544 × 10⁶ = 1665 W m⁻², which is the intensity we started from. Note too that √(1.2558 × 10⁶) is manageable by hand, since 10⁶ roots to 10³ and √1.2558 is about 1.12.

phy-c10-01.background: A transformer trades voltage against current using only the ratio of turns on its two coils. The alternating current in the primary makes a changing flux in the iron core, the core carries that flux to the secondary, and each secondary turn picks up an equal share. More turns therefore means more volts. Nothing is created: what the voltage gains, the current gives up.
given: Ep = 240 V applied to the primary
phy-c10-01.find: Whether it steps up or down, and the secondary voltage Es
phy-c10-01.why: The turns ratio and one voltage are given and the other voltage is wanted. Read the ratio before calculating: Ns is ten times Np, so this is a step UP and the answer must exceed 240 V. That reading alone eliminates most of the options.
symbols: Es = the secondary or output voltage, in volts
Ep = the primary or input voltage, in volts
Ns = turns on the secondary coil
Np = turns on the primary coil
steps: More turns on the secondary, so it STEPS UP
phy-c10-01.check: Decide the direction first and the arithmetic becomes a formality: step up rules out both step-down options immediately, and among what remains the ratio is 10, not 1 and not 100. Remember that stepping the voltage up steps the current DOWN by the same factor, so this transformer would deliver a tenth of the primary current, since power cannot be manufactured by winding wire.
